title: Prayer in the lab
hookLine: a careful study found no benefit from strangers praying for heart patients, and some believers say prayer isn't a lab tool (Benson et al.)

lines: STRANGERS PRAY, AS PART OF A STUDY.
cards: On a card: a first name and a last initial. That's all a small prayer group is handed. Somewhere else, a heart patient is waiting for bypass surgery, and the group has never met this person.
They will pray for them anyway, as part of a study. Another group of patients gets no such prayers. A third group is told, for certain, that strangers are praying for them.
Then the doctors count what happens after surgery, and people of faith and skeptics read the result very differently.

teach.b: First, the study. A team led by the cardiologist Herbert Benson followed patients having heart bypass surgery at several hospitals.
Some were prayed for by groups from religious communities who knew only a first name and a last initial. Some were not. And some were told plainly that they were being prayed for.
Prayer from strangers made no measurable difference to complications after surgery. And the patients told for certain that they were being prayed for had somewhat more complications, not fewer.
The study offers no settled explanation for that. Third, how some believers answered: they shrugged, and kept praying. Their point is older than any lab.
In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus is in the wilderness, dared to throw himself down from the temple so that angels will catch him.
In the King James words, he answers: "It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God."

teach.h: A TRIAL OF GOD AS A DARE?
teach.b: To some readers, a controlled trial of God sounds a little like that dare: set up the test, then wait for heaven to perform. On this view, prayer is a relationship, not a dose of medicine. Fourth, how skeptics answered.
If prayer from far away worked like a drug, a careful trial should catch it, and this one didn't.
Both sides read the same paper.

teach.h: THOU SHALT NOT TEMPT THE LORD THY GOD.
teach.b: One says prayer isn't the kind of thing a lab can weigh. The other says the lab weighed it and found nothing. This path doesn't settle that argument.
It asks you to hold both views with respect.

how: People of faith pray in many ways, for themselves and for others; some say prayer is a relationship with God rather than something a study can measure, while skeptics point to trials that found no effect.

games.q: what does “prayer in the lab” mean?
o: a study proving that prayer heals heart patients faster than medicine
a hospital rule banning prayer groups from visiting surgery patients
a careful trial that found strangers' prayers didn't change surgery outcomes

games.q: prayer in the lab: tap the pairs.
p: led the study of prayer and heart surgery
a first name and last initial
thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God

s: in the study, prayer from strangers made no measurable difference to complications
that was the main result of the trial.
patients told for certain they were prayed for did better
they had somewhat more complications, and the study offers no settled explanation.
every believer saw the study as a blow to faith
some answered that prayer was never meant to be tested like a drug.

games.q: you're in the wilderness, and you're dared to jump from the temple so that angels will catch you. what do you say?
o: refuse: thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.
ask for a smaller test first.
games.why: in Matthew, Jesus refuses the dare. some believers hear a controlled trial of prayer the same way: a test God isn't asked to pass.

practice: On an in-breath, bring up the first view: prayer is a relationship, and a lab can't weigh it. On the out-breath, the second: a careful test looked, and found nothing.
Don't pick a winner; let both sit in the room the way two guests can share a couch, and if you pray, you can pray now as you usually do.

wordCard.voice: Prayer in the lab. A careful trial found no benefit from strangers' prayers for heart patients, and some believers answer that prayer was never a lab tool. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, from Matthew 4:7: "thou shalt tempt," in the sense of putting someone to the test.

carryVoice: Your line: not a lab tool. Both readings of that paper deserve a fair hearing. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Benson et al., "Study of the Therapeutic Effects of Intercessory Prayer (STEP) in cardiac bypass patients" (American Heart Journal)

sources.q: It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God
